intro: The finale gives the preceding movement’s turning figure a new life in slow, densely divided strings. Broad statements repeatedly dissolve into exposed lines, until the last page reduces the orchestra to fragments separated by rests.
question: Does the ending arrive through a final chord, or through the gradual loss of continuous motion?

sections.label: Opening · the string-led subjects
sections.mNote: descending phrases and turns establish the principal material

sections.label: Interlude · exposed lines
sections.mNote: widely separated registers replace the dense string texture

sections.label: Restatement · greater weight
sections.mNote: the principal material returns in stronger contrapuntal combinations

sections.label: Interlude · sustained tones and fragments
sections.mNote: reduced scoring revisits the earlier contrast of high and low

cues.title: Violins before the full strings
cues.text: The two violin sections begin together with a forceful unison line. The other strings enter for the broad, quiet phrase that follows; the opening already contrasts a single contour with densely divided harmony.
cues.evidence: First-edition score, printed p. 164: violins alone in the first two bars, then the full strings at Molto adagio. The report drops after the initial gesture around 0:10–0:15 before rebuilding.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A turn changes its character
cues.text: The small turning figure recalls the preceding movement’s lyrical episode. Here it belongs to a slower, string-led texture: hear the connection as a change of character, not an unchanged quotation.
cues.evidence: The relationship between the Rondo-Burleske’s turn and the finale’s principal material is described by Lew Smoley: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-4-adagio-sehr-langsam-und-noch-zuruckhaltend/
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An exposed low reply
cues.text: Within the first large paragraph, the string texture withdraws to an exposed bassoon line. Its upward movement contrasts with the falling phrases around it, supplying material that will recur in later, quieter interludes.
cues.evidence: The bassoon interlude follows the first string subject on printed p. 164. A strong boundary at 1:24 and low windows at 1:25–1:30 anchor the reduced passage; its first bassoon note is not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two subjects share their materials
cues.text: The opening’s two principal themes both use descending phrases and turns. Listen for these common shapes inside the interweaving string parts; they allow Mahler to combine themes rather than merely alternate them.
cues.evidence: Smoley identifies the shared falling phrases and turn figures of the two principal subjects. This cue does not assign a specific thematic entry or chord to 2:00.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A crest without final rest
cues.text: The opening span reaches a sustained crest, then loses much of its weight. Follow the melodic line through the reduction: a large phrase can continue across a dramatic change of texture.
cues.evidence: High-level windows occur at 2:30–2:35; the report remains elevated through 3:05 before a sharp fall at 3:10. The cue covers this extended crest and approaching withdrawal.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: High and low move apart
cues.text: The quieter interlude separates high sustained violin sound from a rising low line. Contrabassoon and cellos recall the earlier bassoon material, while the thinner texture exposes the distance between the registers.
cues.evidence: Smoley describes the high violin A and low contrabassoon/cello line after the opening span. The report drops at 3:10 and remains comparatively quiet through 4:20; timing is passage-level.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Not the final act of composition
cues.text: Mahler completed the Ninth’s fair copy in 1910, then worked on a Tenth Symphony that summer. The Ninth is his last completed symphony, not the last music he wrote.
cues.evidence: Mahler-Online dates the Ninth’s fair copy to December 1909–April 1910; Ryding’s Library of Congress essay identifies the unfinished Tenth. https://acdh-ch.pages.oeaw.ac.at/muwi/mahler-mei/mahler-wv-static/GMW_050.html
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The bass remains independent
cues.text: In these more exposed textures, follow the low line separately from the upper melody. A rising bass can work against a descending phrase above it, giving the passage direction without restoring the full orchestral weight.
cues.evidence: The score-derived interlude combines upper thematic fragments with a rising low line. The cue is a general way of following the counterpoint, not a precise entry claim.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The principal material regains weight
cues.text: The broad string material returns with renewed force. Its familiar turns and falling phrases now combine across several parts; recognition comes with denser counterpoint rather than a simple repeat of the opening.
cues.evidence: The score and Smoley describe the return and combination of the principal subjects. The strong 5:06 boundary and level rise between 5:00 and 5:05 anchor this broad restatement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sustained notes, moving harmony
cues.text: A long note in one part may stretch over changes in the others. Listen beneath the most prominent melody for these independent movements: the slow tempo does not make the harmony static.
cues.evidence: General score-based observation about the finale’s multi-part string writing. No machine-derived chord label or exact suspension is asserted.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The largest measured crest
cues.text: This broad stretch contains the recording’s highest relative-level windows. The lines remain long even as the sound gains weight; intensity comes from their overlap and harmonic pressure, not simply from quick notes.
cues.evidence: The report lists 6:40, 6:45, 6:55, 7:30 and 7:35 as its highest five-second windows. The description of sustained lines comes from the score; measured level is not equated with written dynamics.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A phrase reaches beyond its crest
cues.text: Listen for the continuation after this sustained high point. Mahler repeatedly denies the expectation that an orchestral crest must be followed by a firm, final cadence.
cues.evidence: Relative level stays high through 7:35, then falls sharply at 7:40 with a strong boundary at 7:42. This identifies the approach to a major withdrawal, not a particular harmonic cadence.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A reduced texture returns
cues.text: The dense writing gives way again to exposed lines and sustained tones. This recalls the earlier interlude’s contrast of registers, but its continuation travels through different instrumental colours and fragments.
cues.evidence: The score’s repeated reductions and second extended interlude are described by Smoley. The 7:42 boundary precedes substantially lower levels through 8:35, supporting the broad section change.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A held note can connect
cues.text: In this movement, a high sustained note often survives after the surrounding texture withdraws. Listen for that note as a link into a new passage, not merely as the last sound of the previous one.
cues.evidence: Smoley traces successive high sustained violin notes that bridge the finale’s sections. This cue explains the recurring technique without identifying one exact onset.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Walter questioned the reissue
cues.text: In 1954, Walter objected to an American reissue made without his knowledge, citing musical and technical shortcomings. The historical importance of this performance should not be confused with the conductor’s unconditional approval of every edition.
cues.evidence: Erik Ryding, Library of Congress essay, pp. 2–3, quotes Walter’s September 1954 letter to George Marek: https://lcweb2.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Colour within a sparse ensemble
cues.text: The middle interlude uses widely spaced strings, individual woodwinds and harp rather than a full string choir throughout. Try following the short replies between registers instead of waiting for one continuous tune.
cues.evidence: Smoley identifies clarinet, harp, cor anglais, flute and low-string figures in the extended interlude. The report’s lower-level 9:25–10:40 region supports the broad placement, not an exact simultaneous roster.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The next accumulation approaches
cues.text: Listen for the quieter fragments to reconnect into longer, stronger lines. The coming rise depends on contrary motion — some parts climb as others fall — as well as on the number of instruments involved.
cues.evidence: The score-derived later development combines ascending and descending material. The report begins a strong rise through 10:45–11:00; the cue anticipates that broad accumulation rather than placing its first bar at 10:40.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Another extended orchestral rise
cues.text: The later build sustains its weight over several phrases. Compare it with the earlier large crest: the same stock of turns and falling intervals can support a new span without being replayed literally.
cues.evidence: The report shows consistently higher levels from 11:00 through 11:50, including crests at 11:25 and 11:40, after the preceding quieter region. The thematic comparison follows the score.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The climax does not end everything
cues.text: At the late climax, forcefully repeated violin notes and descending chromatic lines interrupt the forward climb. The principal material continues beyond this rupture instead of allowing it to serve as a final ending.
cues.evidence: Smoley describes the repeated violin C♭s and following chromatic descent at the development climax. The 11:56 boundary, changed brightness and attack profile at 12:00–12:10 anchor the broad rupture region, not individual notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Familiar shapes inside new combinations
cues.text: As the principal themes are restated, follow their falling steps and turns through the different parts. Their shared shapes make it possible for one line to continue a thought that another has begun.
cues.evidence: Smoley describes the late combination and restatement of the principal subjects. The cue is a general thematic listening point, not a bar-aligned declaration of the recapitulation’s start.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The last large statements
cues.text: The later return still has enough weight for broad statements of the main material. Listen for the contour of the opening inside this fuller setting, before the orchestral texture begins its final withdrawal.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the late principal-theme statements. Boundaries at 13:10 and 13:14 precede high-level windows at 13:15–13:30; another rise at 13:55–14:25 comes before the final reduction.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A last sustained wave
cues.text: One more sustained rise precedes the long closing reduction. It is not followed by a decisive full-orchestra cadence; the movement will let individual lines and fragments finish the work.
cues.evidence: The report remains elevated across 13:55–14:25, then declines through 14:30–14:45. The score establishes that the ending proceeds through reduced forces rather than another full-orchestra finish.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The orchestra begins to withdraw
cues.text: In the closing stretch, exposed wind and string lines replace the full ensemble. The melodic material survives, but its phrases become shorter and increasingly separated from one another.
cues.evidence: The score’s late withdrawal and fragmentation are described by Smoley. The report falls from −11.7 dB at 14:25 to −30.7 at 14:45 and stays comparatively low thereafter.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A documented style of connection
cues.text: Reviewing this 1938 performance, John Quinn draws attention to downward string portamento — audible slides between notes — in the finale’s later pages. Listen for that way of joining pitches, rather than assuming every interval is cleanly separated.
cues.evidence: John Quinn’s review reproduced on Pristine PASC389 discusses downward portamenti late in this performance: https://www.pristineclassical.com/products/pasc389 . Its transfer has different timings; this is a passage-level performance-style prompt, not a claim to have detected a slide in the local features.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Only strings remain
cues.text: The last page is marked “Adagissimo”. Muted second violins resume with a short rising line, and the string parts continue in fragments separated by rests. The opening’s broad continuity has become difficult to sustain.
cues.evidence: Score printed p. 180 shows Adagissimo, muted second violins and the remaining strings. The report’s very low 15:30–15:45 region and subsequent small recoveries support a broad final-page placement; the first note is unaligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mozart shared the concert
cues.text: The surviving programme for 16 January 1938 pairs Mahler’s Ninth with Mozart’s D-major “Prague” Symphony, K. 504. The recording came from the Vienna Philharmonic’s fifth subscription concert of the 1937–38 season.
cues.evidence: International Gustav Mahler Society catalogue of original programme V-002-001296: https://www.gustav-mahler.org/libraryid/10405 . The catalogue names both works, concert number, date, hall, orchestra and conductor.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A song remembered in fragments
cues.text: The ending recalls the phrase “Der Tag ist schön” from the fourth Kindertotenlieder song. It is a musical connection, not proof of a single autobiographical programme: listen for a short remembered shape within the broken string phrases.
cues.evidence: Smoley identifies the late Kindertotenlieder connection in the finale. The cue deliberately does not locate its exact notes in this transfer or convert the song text into Mahler’s declared intention.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An ending without a final stroke
cues.text: The remaining strings arrive at D♭ major without a forceful closing stroke. Listen to how the rests, held notes and releases have already changed your sense of time before the sound finally disappears.
cues.evidence: Score printed p. 180 ends with very quiet string fragments and a final D♭-major sonority. The report has low and separated late windows, falls sharply at 18:20 and reaches near-silence by 18:25 before the 18:30 file end.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A held violin note opens the texture
transitions.how: The broad string paragraph withdraws to a high sustained violin note. Contrabassoon and cellos bring back the rising low line previously introduced by bassoon, separating the registers that the dense string writing had joined. The interlude preserves thematic fragments while changing their spacing and instrumental weight.
transitions.evidence: Smoley describes the high-A bridge and returning low line. This file’s sharp level fall at 3:10 followed by a quieter region anchors the approximate transition.

transitions.title: Separated lines gather into the principal themes
transitions.how: The exposed lines reconnect with the principal string material in the original tempo and D♭-major region. The two main subjects share descending phrases and turns, allowing different parts to combine them contrapuntally. Horn colour adds to the returning string texture rather than announcing an unrelated theme.
transitions.evidence: Score-derived return described by Smoley; the local report marks 5:06 and a pronounced rise at 5:05, followed by sustained D♭-compatible content. The precise written return is not bar-aligned.

transitions.title: The orchestral crest contracts around sustained tones
transitions.how: After the larger crest, the orchestral weight falls away around held violin sound and smaller wind and string replies. The earlier contrast of sustained high register and moving lower lines returns, but the continuation develops different fragments and colours. This is a renewed contrasting region, not a literal repeat of the first interlude.
transitions.evidence: The report falls sharply between 7:35 and 7:40 with a boundary at 7:42. Smoley describes the reduced interlude and surviving high note; the marker covers the broad reduction rather than every internal change.

transitions.title: Contrary-moving fragments rebuild the orchestral argument
transitions.how: The scattered material becomes longer and more strongly connected. Strings rebuild the second subject while lower woodwinds and brass add weight; ascending and descending lines pull against one another. The recurring turn figure ties this later development to the opening without freezing it into a repeated block.
transitions.evidence: Score-derived development described by Smoley. The report’s rise through 10:45–11:00 and sustained higher levels afterwards provide the broad timing anchor.

transitions.title: Familiar contours continue beyond the rupture
transitions.how: The principal subjects continue beyond the late climax in new combinations. Falling phrases and turns remain recognisable across the string and wind parts, while D♭ major again becomes a reference point. This section marker identifies the later large statements, not an exact first bar of a recapitulation.
transitions.evidence: Smoley describes the post-climax thematic restatement. Boundaries at 13:10 and 13:14 and the following 13:15–13:30 rise anchor this editorial late-statement region; its formal onset remains provisional.

transitions.title: The last full statement releases individual lines
transitions.how: The last broad statement relinquishes its orchestral mass. High violins remain above exposed wind replies, including cor anglais, before the material passes down into smaller string fragments. Continuity now depends on held notes and short answers rather than on another full statement of the opening theme.
transitions.evidence: The score-derived closing withdrawal is described by Smoley. Relative level falls through 14:30–14:45 after the 13:55–14:25 crest, anchoring the broad reduction.

transitions.title: A pause leaves the strings to continue
transitions.how: The final reduction reaches a pause, then the last page resumes at Adagissimo with muted second violins. Violas and cellos join the remaining string fragments, with rests interrupting their continuity. The movement prolongs D♭ major through changing inner notes and releases instead of restoring the full orchestra for a decisive cadence.
transitions.evidence: Printed p. 180 supplies Adagissimo, string scoring and separated phrases. Very low windows at 15:30–15:45 and later small recoveries anchor the final-page region without locating its first bar precisely.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; Dover reprint)
source.locator: Movement IV, printed pp. 164–180, especially opening p. 164 and closing p. 180. Intermediate highlights follow the score-derived guide and local feature anchors; timing remains passage-level.

timeline.note: First two bars: both violin sections share the opening line before the other strings enter.
Molto adagio paragraph: full strings, with divided inner parts, replace the initial violin unison.
First reduced bridge: an exposed bassoon line rises beneath the surviving violin tone.
First extended interlude: the low rising line contrasts with the sustained upper register.
Principal-material restatement: strings combine related themes with horn participation.
Extended interlude: successive woodwind replies, harp and widely spaced strings replace a continuous tutti.
Later accumulation: stronger winds and brass join the contrapuntal strings towards the climax.
Closing reduction: exposed wind replies remain briefly around the string lines.
Adagissimo page: strings alone; the initial muted second-violin phrase gives way to separated fragments.
Last-bars preview: the first violins and basses drop out, leaving the inner and lower string voices to release the final sonority.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The recording sources identify the complete movement but do not establish the performing edition or any local alterations. The 1912 full score is used as a structural reference, not proof of the parts on the 1938 desks.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: 16 January is the documented public concert date. Pristine gives 15–16 January 1938 for its reissue; the inspected evidence does not establish whether any rehearsal material entered the issued matrices. The Commons embedded “1962” digitising tag is not accepted as a performance or transfer date.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The source CD catalogue number is unknown. Pristine documents the historical ten-disc HMV set as DB 8569–8578; that does not identify the carrier transferred for Commons.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Pristine lists the original complete-set matrix series 2VH 7027–7046. The inspected DAHR composer listing did not establish a matrix/take match for this digital source; no exhaustive absence is claimed. Specific takes and a verified movement-to-matrix mapping remain unestablished, so the complete-set series is not presented as a side identification for this file.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No engineer for the source CD or Commons transfer is identified. Gaisberg was the original recording producer and Charlie Gregory the recording engineer, not established digital-transfer credits. Andrew Rose’s named 2013 Pristine transfer is a different reissue and is not the source of this Commons upload.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is established. The embedded digitising value 1962 is not corroborated as a transfer date and is not used as one; neither upload nor release dates substitute for it.

fields.value: The underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Mahler died in 1911. This is a term calculation for the composition, not worldwide clearance of an unidentified edition or transfer.

This package is admitted on that territorial recording-rights basis, not merely the composition’s age. United States status is not established; no worldwide public-domain clearance is asserted.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
